All work is in Python. The single training/test split is drawn with seed 432 and shared by both questions. Neighbor weights are equal throughout, and plot formatting is left at library defaults.

Show the workflow 
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score

pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:.4f}")

Question 1: Compare KNN and logistic regression

The 569 rows are permuted once and the first round⁡(0.7⋅569)=398\operatorname{round}(0.7 \cdot 569) = 398 go to training, leaving 171 for testing. Each predictor is centered by its training mean and divided by its training standard deviation (divisor n−1n-1); the test rows reuse those same constants, so no test information enters the fitted models.

Show the workflow 
SEED = 432
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

data = pd.read_csv("data/breast-cancer.csv")
predictors = ["mean_radius", "mean_texture", "mean_smoothness"]
X = data[predictors].to_numpy()
y = data["y"].to_numpy()

idx = rng.permutation(len(y))
n_train = round(0.7 * len(y))
train, test = idx[:n_train], idx[n_train:]

center = X[train].mean(axis=0)
scale = X[train].std(axis=0, ddof=1)
X_train, X_test = (X[train] - center) / scale, (X[test] - center) / scale
y_train, y_test = y[train], y[test]

pd.DataFrame(
    {"n": [len(y_train), len(y_test)],
     "malignant": [y_train.sum(), y_test.sum()],
     "malignant rate": [y_train.mean(), y_test.mean()]},
    index=["training", "test"],
)
n malignant malignant rate
training 398 154 0.3869
test 171 58 0.3392

Logistic regression is fit with penalty="none" (scikit-learn 1.0), so it is the ordinary maximum-likelihood fit with an intercept. For KNN, predict_proba returns the fraction of the kk nearest training points that are malignant, which is the estimate of P(Y=1∣X=x)P(Y=1 \mid X=x).

Show the workflow 
ks_q1 = [5, 15, 25, 35, 45]

models = {"logistic": LogisticRegression(penalty="none").fit(X_train, y_train)}
for k in ks_q1:
    models[f"KNN, k = {k}"] = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k).fit(X_train, y_train)

test_prob = {name: m.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] for name, m in models.items()}
auc_q1 = pd.Series({name: roc_auc_score(y_test, p) for name, p in test_prob.items()},
                   name="test AUC")
auc_q1.to_frame()
test AUC
logistic 0.9820
KNN, k = 5 0.9596
KNN, k = 15 0.9789
KNN, k = 25 0.9755
KNN, k = 35 0.9778
KNN, k = 45 0.9772
Show the workflow 
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for name, p in test_prob.items():
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, p)
    ax.plot(fpr, tpr, label=f"{name} (AUC = {auc_q1[name]:.3f})")
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("1 - specificity")
ax.set_ylabel("sensitivity")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

Preferred model: logistic regression. It has the largest test AUC, 0.982, so it ranks a malignant case above a benign one about 98% of the time. The best KNN fit is k=15k=15 at 0.979. The KNN curves improve sharply from k=5k=5 (0.960), whose estimated probabilities take only six values and are noisy, and then stay flat between 0.976 and 0.979 for kk from 15 to 45. The gap between logistic regression and the best KNN is small for a test set with only 58 malignant cases, so the AUC alone does not separate them decisively. But logistic regression is at least as good, it needs no tuning of kk, and with three predictors a linear log-odds boundary is evidently flexible enough here. Its coefficients also show which measurements push the probability up. KNN offers no advantage in this case to make up for being harder to interpret.

Question 2: Training and test ROC curves

The split and standardization are those of Question 1. Calling predict_proba on the training matrix itself makes each training point its own nearest neighbor at distance zero, which is the self-inclusion the question asks for. No two rows share all three predictor values, so for k=1k=1 every training point’s only neighbor is itself.

Show the workflow 
ks_q2 = [1, 3, 5, 10, 20]

prob_q2, auc_rows = {}, {}
for k in ks_q2:
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k).fit(X_train, y_train)
    prob_q2[k] = {"training": (y_train, knn.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1]),
                  "test": (y_test, knn.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])}
    auc_rows[k] = {s: roc_auc_score(*prob_q2[k][s]) for s in ("training", "test")}

auc_q2 = pd.DataFrame(auc_rows).T.rename_axis("k")
auc_q2["training - test"] = auc_q2["training"] - auc_q2["test"]
auc_q2
training test training - test
k
1 1.0000 0.8523 0.1477
3 0.9903 0.9310 0.0594
5 0.9859 0.9596 0.0263
10 0.9776 0.9706 0.0069
20 0.9786 0.9777 0.0009
Show the workflow 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(6.5, 5.2), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, k in zip(axes.flat, ks_q2):
    for s in ("training", "test"):
        fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(*prob_q2[k][s])
        ax.plot(fpr, tpr, label=f"{s} ({auc_q2.loc[k, s]:.3f})")
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_title(f"k = {k}")
    ax.legend(fontsize="small", loc="lower right")
axes.flat[-1].axis("off")
for ax in axes[1]:
    ax.set_xlabel("1 - specificity")
for ax in axes[:, 0]:
    ax.set_ylabel("sensitivity")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

What the gap shows. Training AUC is always above test AUC, and the gap shrinks quickly as kk grows: 0.148 at k=1k=1, 0.059 at k=3k=3, 0.026 at k=5k=5, and nearly zero by k=20k=20. Test AUC moves the other way, rising from 0.852 to 0.978. The reason is that a training point’s own label is one of the kk labels averaged into its estimate. That label carries weight 1/k1/k, so the estimate leans toward the right answer by construction, and this advantage disappears for a new point, which is never among its own neighbors. A large kk dilutes the self-vote, so training and test estimates come from essentially the same averaging and the two AUCs meet. For kk between 10 and 20, training AUC no longer decreases.

At k=1k=1. Each training point’s estimate is its own label, exactly 0 or 1. So every malignant case is ranked above every benign one, and the training ROC curve jumps straight to the upper-left corner with AUC exactly 1. This only says that the model has memorized the training labels; the response itself was used to make each prediction. A test point instead takes the label of one nearby training point. That estimate is also 0 or 1, so the test ROC curve has a single interior corner (sensitivity and specificity at the cutoff 0.5) joined by straight lines, and the AUC drops to 0.852. One neighbor gives the noisiest possible estimate of p(x)p(x). Training performance therefore cannot be used to judge or tune kk: by that measure k=1k=1 would look best, when it is in fact the worst of the five on new data.

Part 3: Correction

The correction keeps the report’s classifier, its choice of the first three Euclidean errors, and the title format, and changes only the display range to vmin=-1, vmax=1. The pixel files are the Homework 5 course copies.

zip_train = np.loadtxt("../week-05/data/knn/zip-train.csv.gz", delimiter=",")
zip_test = np.loadtxt("../week-05/data/knn/zip-test.csv.gz", delimiter=",")
X5, y5 = zip_train[:1000, 1:], zip_train[:1000, 0].astype(int)
X5_test, y5_test = zip_test[:500, 1:], zip_test[:500, 0].astype(int)

y5_hat = np.zeros(len(y5_test), dtype=int)
for i in range(len(y5_test)):
    d = np.sqrt(np.sum((X5 - X5_test[i]) ** 2, axis=1))
    neighbors = np.argsort(d, kind="stable")[:5]
    y5_hat[i] = np.argmax(np.bincount(y5[neighbors], minlength=10))

incorrect = np.flatnonzero(y5_hat != y5_test)[:3]
plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 2.4))
for l, i in enumerate(incorrect):
    plt.subplot(1, 3, l + 1)
    plt.imshow(zip_test[i, 1:].reshape(16, 16), cmap="gray_r",
               vmin=-1, vmax=1, interpolation="nearest")
    plt.title(f"True: {y5_test[i]} Predicted: {y5_hat[i]}")
    plt.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The three images are again test rows 4, 13, and 14 (true 6, 2, 4; predicted 0, 0, 7), so the report’s written comments on these digits still apply. In the revised GitHub Issue I asked the author to set vmin=-1, vmax=1, regenerate the figure for the same three images, keep the true and predicted labels in the titles, and replace the figure in the report.
